title: CUET Political Science Test 5
subject: Political Science (Code: 323)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Political Science - 323.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) Political Science papers 2024 and 2026, analysed for format only (no questions copied)
textbooks: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence
instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
One set of 5 questions is based on a passage; the set stays together.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Seats won by the Congress in 2004
questions.question: In the 2004 Lok Sabha election, the Congress emerged as the largest party and led the UPA government. About how many seats did the Congress itself win?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 145
Why: The Congress won 145 seats in 2004 and formed the UPA government with allies.
Why not the others:
(A) 282 was the BJP's tally in 2014.
(C) 206 was the Congress's tally in 2009.
(D) 44 was the Congress's tally in 2014.
Key point: Even the winning party needed allies in 2004.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: The coalition era and the growing consensus — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The 2019 Lok Sabha election returned the BJP-led NDA to power.
(B) Most major parties came to agree on the new economic policies.
(C) Most parties accepted the political and social claims of the backward castes.
(D) Alliances came to rest more on practical considerations than on ideology.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B), (C) and (D)
Why: All four are true. (A) the NDA won again in 2019. (B), (C) and (D) are three parts of the consensus NCERT describes in the coalition era.
Why not the others: Options (A), (B) and (C) each leave out at least one true statement.
Key point: Competition rose, but so did a broad consensus on key issues.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Difference between arms control and disarmament
questions.question: How does arms control differ from disarmament?
options: A) Arms control requires all states to give up all their weapons.
B) Arms control applies only to conventional weapons such as tanks.
C) Arms control means a state builds more weapons to deter its rivals.
D) Arms control regulates the acquisition or development of weapons.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Arms control regulates the acquisition or development of weapons.
Why: Arms control regulates the acquisition or development of weapons, while disarmament requires states to give up certain kinds of weapons.
Why not the others:
(A) Giving up weapons is disarmament.
(B) Arms control also covers nuclear weapons.
(C) Building more weapons is the opposite of arms control.
Key point: The ABM Treaty and SALT are examples of arms control.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Meaning of the circle of stars on the EU flag
questions.question: The circle of gold stars on the flag of the European Union stands for:
options: A) solidarity and harmony among the peoples of Europe
B) the number of countries that founded the NATO alliance
C) the twelve months of the year in the European calendar
D) Europe's final victory in the Second World War of 1939–45
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) solidarity and harmony among the peoples of Europe
Why: The circle of gold stars symbolises solidarity and harmony among the peoples of Europe.
Why not the others: (B), (C), (D) The stars do not stand for NATO, months or a war victory.
Key point: The EU has its own flag, anthem and currency.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Environmental landmarks in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) The Kyoto Protocol
(B) The Brundtland Report, 'Our Common Future'
(C) The Antarctic Treaty
(D) The Club of Rome's 'Limits to Growth'
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (D), (B), (A)
Why: (C) The Antarctic Treaty was signed in 1959. (D) 'Limits to Growth' was published in 1972. (B) The Brundtland Report came out in 1987. (A) The Kyoto Protocol was agreed in 1997.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts 'Limits to Growth' before the Antarctic Treaty. Option (B) puts Brundtland before 'Limits to Growth'. Option (D) puts Kyoto before Brundtland.
Key point: 1959 → 1972 → 1987 → 1997.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Why India refused to sign the NPT
questions.question: Why did India refuse to sign the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty?
options: A) It thought the treaty was discriminatory, applying only to non-nuclear states.
B) It was secretly planning a nuclear attack on Pakistan in the near future.
C) Signing the treaty would have forced India to give up its UN membership.
D) The Soviet Union had formally asked India not to sign the treaty at all.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) It thought the treaty was discriminatory, applying only to non-nuclear states.
Why: India saw the NPT as discriminatory: it let the five nuclear powers keep their weapons while barring everyone else.
Why not the others:
(B) India's policy was never one of nuclear attack.
(C) Signing or not signing the NPT has nothing to do with UN membership.
(D) The decision was India's own.
Key point: India opposed the NPT's unequal rules, not disarmament itself.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: India's steps on energy and climate
questions.question:
Match List-I (Indian policy or position) with List-II (What it does or says).

List-I
(A) National Auto-fuel Policy
(B) Energy Conservation Act, 2001
(C) Electricity Act, 2003
(D) India's position on per capita emissions

List-II
(I) Encourages the use of renewable energy
(II) Requires cleaner fuels for vehicles
(III) India's emissions per person stay far below the world average
(IV) Sets out steps to improve energy efficiency
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: The Auto-fuel Policy requires cleaner fuels (II). The Energy Conservation Act aims at energy efficiency (IV). The Electricity Act encourages renewable energy (I). India stresses that its per capita emissions are far below the world average (III).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps the Auto-fuel Policy and the 2001 Act. Option (C) swaps the 2001 and 2003 Acts. Option (D) swaps the 2003 Act and the emissions position.
Key point: India acts on climate while defending its right to develop.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Spotting the traditional threat among four dangers
questions.question: A government lists four dangers it faces. Which one belongs to the traditional idea of security rather than the non-traditional one?
options: A) A war between two states over a border
D) Large-scale migration and refugee flows
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A war between two states over a border
Why: A war between states over territory is the classic traditional threat.
Why not the others: (B), (C), (D) Poverty, epidemics and migration all threaten human security and are non-traditional threats.
Key point: Non-traditional security looks at threats to people, not only to states.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Organisation that sets the rules of global trade
questions.question: Which organisation sets the rules for international trade?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The World Trade Organisation
Why: The WTO sets the rules for global trade.
Why not the others:
(A) UNESCO works for education, science and culture.
(B) Amnesty campaigns for human rights.
(C) The ILO works on labour standards.
Key point: Critics say the WTO's rules favour rich countries.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: First Soviet republic to declare independence
questions.question: In March 1990, which became the first of the fifteen Soviet republics to declare its independence?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Lithuania
Why: Lithuania declared independence in March 1990, the first of the republics to do so.
Why not the others:
(A) Ukraine declared independence later, in 1991.
(C) Kazakhstan was the last to declare independence, in December 1991.
(D) Georgia followed in 1991.
Key point: The Baltic republics led the drive for independence.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Ideas of traditional and non-traditional security
questions.question:
Match List-I (Concept) with List-II (Meaning).

List-I
(A) Deterrence
(B) Defence
(C) Alliance building
(D) Global poverty

List-II
(I) Limiting or ending a war once it has begun
(II) Low incomes and low economic growth in the poorest countries
(III) Preventing war by threatening unacceptable damage
(IV) A coalition of states to deter or defend against attack
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: Deterrence prevents war through the threat of unacceptable damage (III). Defence limits or ends a war that has begun (I). Alliance building forms coalitions of states (IV). Global poverty is a non-traditional threat (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps deterrence and defence. Option (B) swaps defence and alliance building. Option (D) swaps alliance building and global poverty.
Key point: Deterrence and defence are the core of traditional security.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: The Congress as a social and ideological coalition — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Congress began in 1885 as a pressure group of the newly educated, professional and commercial classes.
(B) The Congress accommodated revolutionaries and pacifists, conservatives and radicals.
(C) In the first general election the Congress won more than half of all the votes cast.
(D) The Congress was a social and ideological coalition of many groups.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: (A) the Congress began as a pressure group of the educated classes. (B) it accommodated groups of every kind. (D) NCERT calls it a social and ideological coalition.
Why not the others: (C) is false: the Congress won about 45 per cent of the votes in 1952, but nearly three-fourths of the seats. Options (C) and (D) include (C); option (A) leaves out (D).
Key point: The Congress was a broad umbrella, not a single-ideology party.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Speaker of 'tryst with destiny'
questions.question: Who gave the 'tryst with destiny' speech at midnight on 14–15 August 1947?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Jawaharlal Nehru
Why: Jawaharlal Nehru made the speech in the Constituent Assembly as India became independent.
Why not the others:
(B) Patel was Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister.
(C) Gandhi was in Calcutta, working to stop communal violence.
(D) Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee.
Key point: Nehru's speech set out the challenges facing the new nation.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Pakistan's leaders between 1988 and 1999
questions.question: After General Zia's death, which two leaders alternated as Pakistan's Prime Minister until 1999?
options: A) Zulfikar Ali Bhutto and Ayub Khan
B) Benazir Bhutto and Nawaz Sharif
C) Pervez Musharraf and Yahya Khan
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Benazir Bhutto and Nawaz Sharif
Why: Elected governments led by Benazir Bhutto and Nawaz Sharif alternated in power from 1988 until the 1999 coup.
Why not the others:
(A) Z.A. Bhutto and Ayub Khan belong to earlier decades.
(C) Musharraf and Yahya Khan were military rulers.
(D) Zia was a military ruler; Imran Khan came much later.
Key point: Musharraf's coup in 1999 ended that democratic phase.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Scientist who guided India's nuclear programme
questions.question: India's nuclear programme was started in the late 1940s under the guidance of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Homi J. Bhabha
Why: Homi J. Bhabha guided India's nuclear programme from the late 1940s.
Why not the others:
(A) Raman was a Nobel-winning physicist, not the programme's head.
(C) Sarabhai is linked with the space programme.
(D) Kalam was associated with missiles and came much later.
Key point: Nehru wanted nuclear science for peaceful development.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: States created in 2000 and 2014 and their parent States
questions.question:
Match List-I (New State) with List-II (State it was carved out of).

List-I
(A) Uttarakhand
(B) Chhattisgarh
(C) Jharkhand
(D) Telangana

List-II
(I) Bihar
(II) Andhra Pradesh
(III) Uttar Pradesh
(IV) Madhya Pradesh
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Uttarakhand was carved out of Uttar Pradesh (III), Chhattisgarh out of Madhya Pradesh (IV) and Jharkhand out of Bihar (I), all in 2000. Telangana was carved out of Andhra Pradesh in 2014 (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Madhya Pradesh and Bihar. Option (B) swaps Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh. Option (D) swaps Bihar and Andhra Pradesh.
Key point: The reorganisation of States did not end in 1956.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: India and China, 1949–1964 — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) India was one of the first countries to recognise the Communist government of China.
(B) China took control of Tibet in 1950.
(C) In 1962 China attacked only in the Ladakh region.
(D) Differences over China contributed to the split in the Communist Party of India in 1964.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: in October 1962 China invaded in both disputed areas, Arunachal Pradesh (then NEFA) and Ladakh.
Why not the others: (A) India recognised the People's Republic early. (B) China took over Tibet in 1950. (D) the pro-China group formed the CPI(M) in 1964. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: The 1962 war affected India's politics as well as its defence.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: UN agencies and their fields
questions.question:
Match List-I (UN agency) with List-II (Field of work).

List-I
(A) UNICEF
(B) UNESCO
(C) WHO
(D) UNDP

List-II
(I) Development
(II) Children's welfare
(III) Health
(IV) Education, science and culture
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Why: UNICEF works for children (II). UNESCO works for education, science and culture (IV). WHO works for health (III). UNDP works for development (I).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps UNICEF and UNESCO. Option (B) swaps UNESCO and WHO. Option (C) swaps WHO and UNDP.
Key point: Specialised agencies carry out much of the UN's work.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Which was NOT a result of China's reforms
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a result of China's economic reforms?
options: B) The gap between coastal and inland regions disappeared.
C) Environmental damage and corruption increased.
D) The benefits of growth did not reach everyone equally.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The gap between coastal and inland regions disappeared.
Why: The reforms widened, not removed, the gap between rural and urban areas and between the coast and the interior.
Why not the others:
(A) NCERT notes rising unemployment.
(C) It notes environmental damage and corruption.
(D) It notes that benefits did not reach everyone.
Key point: China's growth has been rapid but uneven.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: India's complaint about Bangladesh's energy policy
questions.question: Which of the following has been a cause of India's unhappiness with Bangladesh?
options: A) Bangladesh's decision to leave SAARC and join ASEAN instead
B) Bangladesh's claim over the Siachen glacier in the Himalaya
C) Bangladesh's refusal to allow the export of natural gas to India
D) Bangladesh's refusal to accept the Indus Waters Treaty with India
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Bangladesh's refusal to allow the export of natural gas to India
Why: India has been unhappy with Bangladesh's refusal to allow the export of natural gas to India, and with its stand on illegal migration.
Why not the others:
(A) Bangladesh is still in SAARC.
(B) Siachen is an India–Pakistan issue; Bangladesh has no claim there.
(D) The Indus treaty is between India and Pakistan.
Key point: India and Bangladesh cooperate on many issues but differ on some.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Largest opposition party in the first Lok Sabha
questions.question: Which party won 16 seats in the first general election and became the largest opposition party in the first Lok Sabha?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Communist Party of India
Why: The CPI won 16 seats in 1952 and emerged as the largest opposition party.
Why not the others:
(B) The Jana Sangh won only 3 seats.
(C) The Socialist Party won many votes but fewer seats.
(D) The KMPP was a smaller party.
Key point: The opposition was small and divided in the first Lok Sabha.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Politics in South Asia's neighbours — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Bhutan is a monarchy whose king has initiated a move towards multi-party democracy.
(B) In 1990 the king of Nepal accepted the demand for a new democratic constitution.
(C) Sheikh Mujib-ur-Rahman was assassinated in August 1975.
(D) Sri Lanka has had long periods of military rule since independence.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false: despite its ethnic conflict, Sri Lanka has kept a democratic political system since independence.
Why not the others: (A) Bhutan's king started the move to democracy. (B) Nepal's king accepted a democratic constitution in 1990. (C) Mujib was killed in a military coup in 1975. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a true statement as false.
Key point: South Asia's record with democracy is mixed.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: How the 1967 election results were described
questions.question: The results of the 1967 general election were so dramatic that political observers described them as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) a political earthquake
Why: In 1967 the Congress lost power in many States and its Lok Sabha majority fell sharply, which observers called a political earthquake.
Why not the others:
(A) 'Silent revolution' is used for the rise of backward castes later.
(B) 'Garage sale' refers to Russian privatisation.
(C) The 'grand alliance' was the opposition coalition of 1971.
Key point: 1967 broke the Congress's grip in the States.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Soviet leaders and what they are known for
questions.question:
Match List-I (Soviet leader) with List-II (Known for).

List-I
(A) Vladimir Lenin
(B) Joseph Stalin
(C) Nikita Khrushchev
(D) Leonid Brezhnev

List-II
(I) Forced collectivisation of agriculture and rapid industrialisation
(II) Criticism of Stalin's style and the idea of peaceful coexistence
(III) The invasion of Afghanistan
(IV) Leading the Bolshevik revolution of 1917
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)
Why: Lenin led the 1917 revolution (IV). Stalin forced collectivisation and rapid industrialisation (I). Khrushchev criticised Stalin and proposed peaceful coexistence (II). Brezhnev's government invaded Afghanistan in 1979 (III).
Why not the others: Option (B) swaps Stalin and Khrushchev. Option (C) swaps Lenin and Stalin. Option (D) swaps Khrushchev and Brezhnev.
Key point: Each leader left a distinct mark on the Soviet system.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: Landmarks of planning and the economy in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) Nationalisation of fourteen private banks
(B) Setting up of the Planning Commission
(C) Start of the Second Five Year Plan
(D) Replacement of the Planning Commission by the NITI Aayog
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (B), (C), (A), (D)
Why: (B) The Planning Commission was set up in March 1950. (C) The Second Plan began in 1956. (A) Fourteen banks were nationalised in 1969. (D) The NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in 2015.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts bank nationalisation before the Second Plan. Option (B) puts the Second Plan before 1950. Option (C) puts the NITI Aayog before 1969.
Key point: 1950 → 1956 → 1969 → 2015.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: How critics described Indira Gandhi in her early years
questions.question: In her first years as Prime Minister, Indira Gandhi was dismissed by some opponents as a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 'goongi gudia' (dumb doll)
Why: Her early critics mocked her as a 'goongi gudia', a dumb doll. She soon proved them wrong.
Why not the others:
(B) 'Iron man' was used for Sardar Patel.
(C) 'Netaji' is used for Subhas Chandra Bose.
(D) 'Deshbandhu' was the title of C.R. Das.
Key point: Indira Gandhi went on to dominate the Congress.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Participation in the Rio Summit
questions.question: About how many states took part in the Earth Summit at Rio de Janeiro in 1992?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 170
Why: The Rio Summit was attended by 170 states, thousands of NGOs and many multinational corporations.
Why not the others:
(B) 51 states founded the UN.
(C) 15 is the size of the Security Council.
(D) 193 is the present UN membership.
Key point: Rio made the environment a central issue of world politics.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: The Ayodhya dispute — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Babri Masjid at Ayodhya was built in the sixteenth century by Mir Baqi, a general of Babur.
(B) The mosque was demolished in December 1990.
(C) In February 1986 the Faizabad district court ordered the locks of the building to be opened.
(D) After the demolition, the Central Government dismissed the BJP governments in several States.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false: the mosque was demolished on 6 December 1992.
Why not the others: (A) NCERT says Mir Baqi built it in the sixteenth century. (C) the Faizabad court ordered the locks opened in 1986. (D) the BJP State governments were dismissed after the demolition. Options (A), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Ayodhya raised serious questions about secularism.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Why the IMF and World Bank are called Bretton Woods institutions
questions.question: The IMF and the World Bank are often called the 'Bretton Woods institutions' because:
options: A) their headquarters are located in the small town of Bretton Woods
B) they were planned at a conference held at Bretton Woods, USA, in 1944
C) they were named after the first President of the World Bank
D) they lend money only to the countries of North America and Europe
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) they were planned at a conference held at Bretton Woods, USA, in 1944
Why: The two institutions were planned at the 1944 conference at Bretton Woods in the USA.
Why not the others:
(A) Both have their headquarters in Washington.
(C) Bretton Woods is a place, not a person's name.
(D) They lend worldwide.
Key point: Both were created to manage the post-war world economy.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: Main criticism of the Second Plan's strategy
questions.question: Critics of the Second Five Year Plan argued that its strategy:
options: A) gave too much money to village industries
B) depended entirely on foreign private capital
C) neglected agriculture in favour of heavy industry
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) neglected agriculture in favour of heavy industry
Why: Many critics felt the Second Plan's push for heavy industry left agriculture short of attention and investment.
Why not the others:
(A) The emphasis was on heavy industry, not village industries.
(B) The plan relied heavily on the public sector.
(D) It expanded the public sector.
Key point: The neglect of agriculture was a major criticism of early planning.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Where backward-class reservations existed before Mandal
questions.question: Before the Mandal Commission's report was implemented, reservations for backward classes already existed:
options: A) only in central government jobs, under the original Constitution
B) only in the north-eastern States, under special provisions
C) in the southern States, since the 1960s if not earlier
D) nowhere in India, since the Constitution did not allow them
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) in the southern States, since the 1960s if not earlier
Why: The southern States had reservations for backward classes since the 1960s if not earlier; the Mandal issue was about central government jobs and the north.
Why not the others:
(A) Central jobs got OBC reservations only after 1990.
(B) The north-eastern States are not the example NCERT gives.
(D) The southern States already had them.
Key point: Mandal brought OBC politics to the national stage.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Japan's military spending as a share of GDP
questions.question: Japan's military expenditure is about what share of its GDP?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1 per cent
Why: Japan spends only about 1 per cent of its GDP on the military, yet because its economy is so large, its spending is among the world's highest.
Why not the others: (A), (B), (D) These shares are far higher than Japan's.
Key point: Japan's power is mainly economic.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Terms from the Emergency period
questions.question:
Match List-I (Term) with List-II (Meaning).

List-I
(A) Preventive detention
(B) Habeas corpus
(C) Press censorship
(D) Total Revolution

List-II
(I) Government approval of news before it is published
(II) Arrest of a person on the fear that he or she may commit an offence
(III) A court order to produce a detained person before a judge
(IV) Jayaprakash Narayan's call for a complete change of society and politics
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV)
Why: Preventive detention is arrest on the fear of a future offence (II). Habeas corpus asks a court to have a detained person produced (III). Press censorship means prior approval of news (I). Total Revolution was JP's call (IV).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps preventive detention and habeas corpus. Option (C) swaps habeas corpus and censorship. Option (D) swaps censorship and Total Revolution.
Key point: During the Emergency, citizens lost the right to move the courts for habeas corpus.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Steps towards the United Nations in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following steps towards the founding of the UN in chronological order:
(A) The San Francisco conference on the UN Charter
(B) The Atlantic Charter
(C) The UN comes into being on 24 October
(D) The Declaration by United Nations
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (B), (D), (A), (C)
Why: (B) The Atlantic Charter was signed in August 1941. (D) The Declaration by United Nations came in January 1942. (A) The San Francisco conference met from April to June 1945. (C) The UN came into being on 24 October 1945.
Why not the others: Option (B) swaps the Atlantic Charter and the Declaration. Option (C) puts San Francisco before the Declaration. Option (D) puts UN Day before the conference.
Key point: 1941 → 1942 → 1945 → 24 October 1945.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Events from 1973 to 1977 in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
(A) The Allahabad High Court sets aside Indira Gandhi's election
(B) The Janata Party is formed
(C) The Supreme Court decides the Kesavananda Bharati case
(D) Students in Gujarat begin an agitation against rising prices
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (D), (A), (B)
Why: (C) The Kesavananda Bharati case was decided in April 1973. (D) The Gujarat agitation began in January 1974. (A) The Allahabad verdict came on 12 June 1975. (B) The Janata Party was formed in January 1977.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts the Gujarat agitation before Kesavananda. Option (B) puts the Allahabad verdict before the Gujarat agitation. Option (D) puts the Janata Party before the Allahabad verdict.
Key point: 1973 → 1974 → 1975 → 1977.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Nature of the Soviet economy
questions.question: What kind of economy did the Soviet Union have?
options: A) A free-market economy with little state role
B) A mixed economy led by private companies
C) A planned economy controlled by the state
D) A barter economy without money
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A planned economy controlled by the state
Why: The Soviet economy was planned and controlled by the state, and land and productive assets were owned by the state.
Why not the others:
(A) Markets had little role.
(B) There was no significant private sector.
(D) The Soviet Union used money.
Key point: State ownership and planning defined the Soviet system.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Which was NOT a cause of the Soviet collapse
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a cause of the disintegration of the Soviet Union?
options: A) Economic stagnation and shortages of consumer goods
B) Heavy spending on weapons and on its satellite states
C) Nationalism and the demand for sovereignty in the republics
D) A defeat of the Soviet army by NATO in a direct war
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A defeat of the Soviet army by NATO in a direct war
Why: The Soviet Union never fought a direct war with NATO; it collapsed from within.
Why not the others:
(A) Economic stagnation was a major cause.
(B) The arms race and support for satellites drained resources.
(C) Nationalism in the republics broke the union apart.
Key point: The Soviet Union fell without a war.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Glacier disputed between India and Pakistan
questions.question: Which glacier is a subject of dispute between India and Pakistan?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Siachen
Why: India and Pakistan dispute control of the Siachen glacier.
Why not the others: (B), (C), (D) Gangotri, Zemu and Pindari are glaciers wholly inside India.
Key point: Siachen is one of several India–Pakistan disputes beyond Kashmir.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Why linguistic reorganisation was first postponed
questions.question: The Congress had promised in the 1920s to reorganise provinces on the basis of language. Why did the national leadership postpone this after Independence?
options: A) Because the new Constitution banned the creation of States based on language
B) Because, after Partition, leaders feared it might cause disintegration
C) Because the princely states had not yet been merged with the Indian Union
D) Because the British had objected to it in their final years of rule
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Because, after Partition, leaders feared it might cause disintegration
Why: The memory of Partition made Nehru and other leaders fear that linguistic States could encourage division.
Why not the others:
(A) The Constitution had no such ban.
(C) The princely states had largely been integrated by then.
(D) The British had left; their views did not decide the matter.
Key point: Popular movements, starting in Andhra, changed the leaders' minds.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: How some newspapers protested against censorship
questions.question: How did newspapers such as the Indian Express and the Statesman protest against press censorship during the Emergency?
options: A) They stopped printing altogether for nineteen months.
B) They moved their offices outside India.
C) They published only foreign news.
D) They left blank spaces where news items had been censored.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) They left blank spaces where news items had been censored.
Why: When news was censored, these papers left the space blank, which itself told readers that something had been suppressed.
Why not the others:
(A) They kept publishing.
(B) They did not move abroad.
(C) They did not switch to foreign news only.
Key point: Blank spaces became a silent protest.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Indian forum against neo-liberal globalisation
questions.question: Which Indian forum, modelled on the World Social Forum, raised voices against neo-liberal globalisation?
options: D) The Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The Indian Social Forum
Why: The Indian Social Forum brought together groups critical of neo-liberal globalisation.
Why not the others:
(B) The Planning Commission was a government body.
(C) The NDC was a government body of Chief Ministers.
(D) FICCI represents business.
Key point: Resistance to globalisation in India came from the left, unions and social movements.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Features and effects of globalisation — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Globalisation involves flows of ideas, capital, commodities and people.
(B) The movement of people across borders has not been globalised to the same degree as the movement of goods.
(C) Some critics fear that cultural globalisation leads to the 'McDonaldisation' of the world.
(D) Globalisation has affected all countries and all sections of society equally.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) NCERT names these four flows. (B) developed countries guard their borders with visa rules. (C) critics fear cultural homogenisation, or McDonaldisation.
Why not the others: (D) is false: globalisation has affected countries and groups very unevenly. Options (C) and (D) include (D); option (B) leaves out (B).
Key point: Globalisation is uneven in what flows and whom it benefits.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: The EU's military strength
questions.question: Which statement best describes the European Union's military strength?
options: A) The EU has no armed forces at all.
B) The EU's forces are smaller than those of any single Asian country.
C) The EU depends entirely on Russia for its defence.
D) The EU's combined armed forces are the second largest in the world.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The EU's combined armed forces are the second largest in the world.
Why: The EU's combined armed forces are the second largest in the world, and its defence spending is second only to the USA's.
Why not the others:
(A) Its members have large armed forces.
(B) Combined, they are among the biggest.
(C) The EU does not depend on Russia.
Key point: The EU is a military as well as an economic power.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Why the Congress dominated the first elections
questions.question: What was the main reason for the Congress's dominance in the first general elections?
options: A) All the other parties had been banned from contesting the first elections.
B) Only the Congress put up candidates who could read and write.
C) The Election Commission was controlled by the ruling Congress party.
D) It carried the national movement's legacy and had a countrywide organisation.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) It carried the national movement's legacy and had a countrywide organisation.
Why: The Congress carried the prestige of the freedom struggle and was the only party with a network of units across the country.
Why not the others:
(A) No party was banned.
(B) Literacy was not a condition for candidates.
(C) The Election Commission was independent.
Key point: Legacy plus organisation explains the Congress's early dominance.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Headquarters of the UN
questions.question: Where are the headquarters of the United Nations?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) New York
Why: The UN's headquarters are in New York.
Why not the others:
(A) Geneva hosts several UN offices and the WTO.
(B) The Hague hosts the International Court of Justice.
(D) Paris hosts UNESCO.
Key point: Several UN bodies are spread across other cities.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Origin of the party that led the Punjabi Suba movement
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

The Akali Dal, formed in 1920 as the political wing of the Sikhs, had led the movement for a Punjabi-speaking State, and in 1966 a smaller Punjab was carved out of the old State. In the 1970s a section of the Akalis began to press for greater autonomy for the region, and by the early 1980s armed militants had made the Golden Temple at Amritsar their base. In June 1984 the Government of India sent the army into the shrine to flush them out. The operation succeeded in its military aim but deeply hurt Sikh sentiment, and it was followed by Indira Gandhi's assassination and violence against Sikhs in Delhi and elsewhere. After the 1984 elections, Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi opened talks with moderate Akali leaders. In July 1985 he and Harchand Singh Longowal signed an agreement. It provided that Chandigarh would be transferred to Punjab, that a separate commission would settle the border dispute with Haryana, that a tribunal would decide how the waters of the Ravi and Beas would be shared among Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan, that people affected by militancy would be compensated, and that the Armed Forces Special Powers Act would be withdrawn from Punjab. Peace did not come quickly. When elections were held in 1992, only about a quarter of the voters turned out. Normal political life returned slowly, and by the middle of the 1990s Punjab had moved back towards peace.

Question: According to the passage, the Akali Dal was formed in 1920 as:
options: A) the political wing of the Sikhs
B) the Punjab branch of the Indian National Congress
C) a trade union of Punjab's farmers
D) a militant group based in the Golden Temple
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) the political wing of the Sikhs
Why: The passage says the Akali Dal was formed in 1920 as the political wing of the Sikhs, and it led the Punjabi Suba movement.
Why not the others:
(B) It was a separate party, not part of the Congress.
(C) It was not a trade union.
(D) The militants of the 1980s were a later, different force.
Key point: The Akali Dal is one of India's oldest regional parties.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Purpose of the army action of June 1984
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Peace did not come quickly. When elections were held in 1992, only about a quarter of the voters turned out. Normal political life returned slowly, and by the middle of the 1990s Punjab had moved back towards peace.

Question: What was the purpose of the army action of June 1984 described in the passage?
options: A) To defend Punjab's border against an attack from Pakistan
B) To remove the Akali government from power in the State
C) To flush armed militants out of the Golden Temple at Amritsar
D) To stop the transfer of Chandigarh from Punjab to Haryana
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) To flush armed militants out of the Golden Temple at Amritsar
Why: The passage says the army was sent into the Golden Temple to flush out militants who had made it their base. This was Operation Blue Star.
Why not the others:
(A) No attack from Pakistan is mentioned.
(B) The aim was to remove militants, not a government.
(D) Chandigarh's transfer came up only in the 1985 accord.
Key point: Operation Blue Star succeeded militarily but deeply hurt Sikh sentiment.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: What the accord said about Chandigarh
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Question: Under the agreement of July 1985 described in the passage, Chandigarh was to be:
options: C) shared as a capital with Rajasthan
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) transferred to Punjab
Why: The passage says the agreement provided that Chandigarh would be transferred to Punjab.
Why not the others:
(A) No new State was proposed.
(C) Rajasthan figures only in the sharing of river waters.
(D) The agreement gave Chandigarh to Punjab, not Haryana.
Key point: Chandigarh has remained a shared capital and a Union Territory, because the transfer was never carried out.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Which was NOT a provision of the Rajiv–Longowal Accord
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Normal political life returned slowly, and by the middle of the 1990s Punjab had moved back towards peace.

Question: Which of the following was NOT a provision of the 1985 agreement, according to the passage?
options: A) A tribunal to decide the sharing of the Ravi and Beas waters
B) A separate commission to settle the border dispute with Haryana
C) Compensation for people affected by militancy
D) Wider special powers for the armed forces in Punjab
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Wider special powers for the armed forces in Punjab
Why: The agreement said the Armed Forces Special Powers Act would be withdrawn from Punjab, not that the army would get wider powers.
Why not the others:
(A) The passage lists a tribunal on the Ravi and Beas waters.
(B) It lists a commission on the border with Haryana.
(C) It lists compensation for victims of militancy.
Key point: The accord sought to restore normal civil government in Punjab.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: What the 1992 turnout suggests
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

The Akali Dal, formed in 1920 as the political wing of the Sikhs, had led the movement for a Punjabi-speaking State, and in 1966 a smaller Punjab was carved out of the old State. In the 1970s a section of the Akalis began to press for greater autonomy for the region, and by the early 1980s armed militants had made the Golden Temple at Amritsar their base. In June 1984 the Government of India sent the army into the shrine to flush them out. The operation succeeded in its military aim but deeply hurt Sikh sentiment, and it was followed by Indira Gandhi's assassination and violence against Sikhs in Delhi and elsewhere. After the 1984 elections, Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi opened talks with moderate Akali leaders. In July 1985 he and Harchand Singh Longowal signed an agreement. It provided that Chandigarh would be transferred to Punjab, that a separate commission would settle the border dispute with Haryana, that a tribunal would decide how the waters of the Ravi and Beas would be shared among Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan, that people affected by militancy would be compensated, and that the Armed Forces Special Powers Act would be withdrawn from Punjab. Peace did not come quickly. When elections were held in 1992, only about a quarter of the voters turned out. Normal political life returned slowly, and by the middle of the 1990s Punjab had moved back towards peace.

Question: The passage says only about a quarter of the voters turned out in the 1992 elections in Punjab. What can best be inferred from this?
options: A) Most people in Punjab supported the militants' demand for a boycott of democracy.
B) The Election Commission had removed most voters from the rolls.
C) Normal democratic politics had not yet fully returned to the State.
D) Punjab had already achieved complete peace by 1992.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Normal democratic politics had not yet fully returned to the State.
Why: The passage links the low turnout to the fact that peace did not come quickly; normal political life returned only slowly.
Why not the others:
(A) The passage does not say most people supported the militants.
(B) Nothing is said about voter rolls.
(D) The passage says peace came only by the mid-1990s.
Key point: A low turnout showed that the return to normal politics was slow.
